title: The wedding date is written
hook: Sohila's first hymn speaks of death as a wedding day already fixed, asking friends for blessing (Gauri Deepaki, ang 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, birha, the ache of separation. Your line was longing is love too. Did missing someone remind you what you love? Today, the bride again, and the day her waiting ends. Day two hundred forty-six.

In an old Punjabi wedding, before the bride leaves her parents' home, there's a small ritual. The women of the family pour a little oil on the threshold, and friends crowd around her with blessings. Everyone knows the date. It was fixed long ago, written down, sent out. Now, hold that picture, because every night, at bedtime, many Sikhs sing a hymn that uses exactly this scene. And the wedding it's talking about is not the one you'd expect. Today: the wedding date is written.
screen: `OIL ON THE THRESHOLD.` → `FRIENDS BRING BLESSINGS.` → `THE DATE WAS FIXED LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: Kirtan Sohila is the Sikh night prayer, five short hymns sung before sleep. It's also sung at the end of a Sikh funeral. Its first hymn is by Guru Nanak, in Rag Gauri Deepaki, on Ang 12. And its central line, in the original, is this: sanbat saahaa likhiaa mil kar paavahu tel. The year and the day are written; come together, friends, and pour the oil. Then: give me your blessings, so that I may meet my Lord. The bride is the soul. The groom is God. And the wedding day, fixed and written, is the day of death. It sounds heavy. It isn't meant to be. Notice what the hymn doesn't do. It doesn't threaten. It doesn't describe punishments. It turns death into a homecoming, the day the long-waiting bride from last week finally goes to her beloved. The hymn adds that this summons comes to every house, every day, and so it asks us to remember the One who calls. That's why it's sung at night. Sleep is a small rehearsal of letting go. You lie down not knowing, trusting the morning. And at a funeral, the same words tell the family: this was not a thief in the night. It was a date, written, and a wedding. And the hymn is honest about its limit: it doesn't say when anyone's day is. Only that it's written, and that the wise way to live is to remember it gently, with friends and blessing.
screen: `KIRTAN SOHILA — THE NIGHT PRAYER.` · `SANBAT SAAHAA — THE DATE IS SET.` · `DEATH AS A WEDDING, NOT A THREAT.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL LETTING GO.` · then, large: `THE DATE IS WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle. Let yourself remember, calmly, that your days are counted, as everyone's are. Not to frighten yourself: just to see today clearly. Then think of one thing you'd want to have done, or said, if you knew the date. A thank-you, an apology, a call. Hold it lightly. Let the breath be slow, the way it is before sleep. The bell holds the time.
The wedding date is written. From Kirtan Sohila's first hymn: death pictured as the soul's wedding day, already fixed, met with friends and blessing rather than fear.
screen: `THE WEDDING DATE IS WRITTEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the date is written. Today, do the one thing you thought of, the thank-you or the call, and don't leave it for someday. Day two hundred forty-six.

screen: `DAY 246 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FROM WOMAN WE ARE BORN.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite or sing Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and it is also recited when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed for the night and at the end of a Sikh funeral.

fork.setup: you're the bride, and the date is written. what does the hymn ask of your friends?
options: gather, pour the oil, and give you their blessings.
fork.reveal: mil kar paavahu tel: come together and pour the oil, and bless me, so that I may meet my Lord.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saha, the fixed wedding date; sanbat saahaa likhiaa, the year and the day are written.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bedtime prayer is about sleeping well.
what it means: Sohila's first hymn pictures death as a wedding day already fixed, so every night becomes a calm remembering.
what a scholar hears: Gauri Deepaki Mahala 1, Ang 12; the oil-pouring alludes to a Punjabi pre-wedding custom at the bride's threshold, and saha is the astrologically fixed date.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (Kirtan Sohila, Gauri Deepaki Mahala 1)
sources.quoted: sanbat saahaa likhiaa mil kar paavahu tel

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (same hymn: the summons comes to every house; remember the One who calls)

notes: Word is the title's head per the outline (no separate word); the word screen shows it in full.
Transliteration 'sanbat saahaa likhiaa mil kar paavahu tel' and the paraphrase of the following line (deh sajan aseesareeaa jio hovai saahib sio mel) should be confirmed.
The oil-pouring (tel chona) as a pre-wedding custom at the bride's door is the usual explanation; confirm.
howItsDone: Sohila recited at night, at the closing of the Guru Granth Sahib (sukhasan), and at the end of a funeral; confirm per the Rehat Maryada.
